Source opened and read: arXiv 2508.10391, "LeanRAG: Knowledge-Graph-Based Generation with Semantic Aggregation and Hierarchical Retrieval" (title matches the citation exactly). Every element of the claim is stated verbatim in the abstract, verified via two independent fetches.

(1) Semantic aggregation = cluster entities + build explicit cross-cluster relations — CONFIRMED: "LeanRAG first employs a novel semantic aggregation algorithm that forms entity clusters and constructs new explicit relations among aggregation-level summaries, creating a fully navigable semantic network."

(2) Bottom-up structure-guided retrieval over a KG — CONFIRMED: "a bottom-up, structure-guided retrieval strategy anchors queries to the most relevant fine-grained entities and then systematically traverses the graph's semantic pathways to gather concise yet contextually comprehensive evidence sets."

(3) Reduces retrieval redundancy by 46% — CONFIRMED: "...while reducing 46% retrieval redundancy."

(4) Outperforms prior methods on 4 QA benchmarks — CONFIRMED: "Extensive experiments on four challenging QA benchmarks with different domains demonstrate that LeanRAG significantly outperforming existing methods in response quality..."

(5) Explicitly fixes two GraphRAG failure modes — 'semantic islands' and retrieval degenerating into flat search that ignores topology — CONFIRMED: "high-level conceptual summaries exist as disconnected `semantic islands', lacking the explicit relations needed for cross-community reasoning; and the retrieval process itself remains structurally unaware, often degenerating into an inefficient flat search that fails to exploit the graph's rich topology."

Attempt to refute: The only slight looseness is the claim's parenthetical gloss "disconnected community summaries" — the abstract says "high-level conceptual summaries" as disconnected semantic islands (and references "cross-community reasoning"), so the gloss is an accurate paraphrase, not a distortion. No sub-claim could be refuted; all figures and framing match the primary source.

Verified against the full HTML of Stream RAG (arXiv:2510.02044v1, "Stream RAG: Instant and Accurate Spoken Dialogue Systems with Streaming Tool Usage"). Every component of the claim matches the source:

(1) CRAG base / 2,706 text queries — CONFIRMED. Paper: "We begin with the CRAG dataset (Yang et al., 2024), which contains 2,706 text queries." AudioCRAG is described as "a benchmark created by converting queries from the publicly available CRAG dataset into speech form."

(2) AudioCRAG-Synthetic = 1,862 TTS queries, Whisper WER=0 filter, UTMOS>=3.5 filter — CONFIRMED. All 2,706 queries were run through an in-house TTS system, then filtered to 1,862 "high-quality spoken queries" by "excluding any utterances for which Whisper hypotheses exhibit a non-zero word error rate" (i.e. keep WER=0) and removing "utterances with suboptimal audio quality, as determined by UTMOS scores below 3.5" (i.e. keep UTMOS>=3.5).

(3) AudioCRAG-Human = 618 human recordings — CONFIRMED. Paper: "we introduce the AudioCRAG-Human benchmark, which consists of 618 human-recorded spoken queries." The abstract independently corroborates both "1,862 TTS-generated queries" and "618 human-recorded queries."

(4) 569 queries rewritten for naturalness — CONFIRMED. Queries "containing dates or brackets" were rewritten "to ensure naturalness and clarity in spoken form": "we identify 569 such queries and rewrite them using a large language model (LLAMA-4 Maverick)."

Source fetched from arxiv.org/abs/2510.02044 (abstract) and arxiv.org/html/2510.02044v1 (full text). The claim's framing of WER=0 (kept = zero-WER) and UTMOS>=3.5 (kept = at/above 3.5) is the correct complement of the paper's exclusion phrasing. No discrepancies found.

The cited source — MarkTechPost, "Google Introduces Speech-to-Retrieval (S2R)...", dated 2025-10-12 — opened successfully (the exact URL in the prompt 404'd, but the real article resolves at the "google-introduces..." slug), and I cross-checked it against the primary Google Research blog ("Speech-to-Retrieval (S2R): A new approach to voice search"). (1) Direct embedding: "S2R maps a spoken query directly to an embedding and retrieves information without first converting speech to text." (MarkTechPost)

(2) Audio query-encoder jointly trained vs. separate document-encoder: "At the heart of our S2R model is a dual-encoder architecture... An audio encoder processes the raw audio of a query... In parallel, a document encoder learns a similar vector representation," trained so "the vector for an audio query is geometrically close to the vectors of its corresponding documents." (Google blog)

(3) Retrieves without ASR: "directly interprets and retrieves information from a spoken query without the intermediate, and potentially flawed, step of having to create a perfect text transcript." (Google blog)

Source opened and read: "Dissecting Agentic RAG: A Component Ablation for Multi-Hop QA with a Local 7B Model" (Sheroz Shaikh), arXiv:2606.21553 — abstract page (https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.21553) and full HTML (https://arxiv.org/html/2606.21553) both fetched successfully.

Every load-bearing element of the claim matches the source:

Loop is the dominant primitive: reducing the retrieval loop to a single step (steps-1) incurs −7.1 EM / −7.6 F1, p<0.001 (McNemar's exact test), described by the authors as "the largest single-component drop in our study" — dwarfing decomposition (−1.4 EM), reranking (−1.7 EM), routing (±0.2 EM). Minor phrasing note (not a defect): the claim says "removing" the loop; the paper operationalizes this as reducing the loop to a single step (steps-1), i.e. removing the iteration — a faithful characterization. No numbers or attribution are misstated.

evidence:
Source located and read: arXiv:2505.00028 "Enhancing Speech-to-Speech Dialogue Modeling with End-to-End Retrieval-Augmented Generation" (Feng, Ma, Chen, Li, Wang, Yu, Chen), EMNLP 2025 Findings. Verified via arxiv.org/abs, the full HTML (arxiv.org/html/2505.00028v1), and the authors' repo github.com/the-bird-F/GLM-Voice-RAG.

Each element of the claim checks out against the paper's own words:

1) Shared-space SONAR retrieval — CONFIRMED. "we adopt SONAR as the encoder function φ, which comprises modality-specific encoders for text (φtext) and speech (φspeech)"; "our method leverages a pretrained embedding model with multiple encoders, allowing both speech queries and textual data to be indexed within the same vector space." So speech queries + text documents go into ONE shared space, enabling direct speech→text retrieval (paper: "directly retrieves relevant textual knowledge from speech queries, eliminating the need for intermediate speech-to-text conversion via ASR").

2) Frozen / no fine-tuning — CONFIRMED (supported, though paper never uses the literal word "frozen"). SONAR is used off-the-shelf ("pretrained embedding model") and GLM-4-Voice is used as the fixed generator ("we employed the end-to-end speech-to-speech dialogue model GLM-4-Voice as the generator"). No training/fine-tuning pipeline for either component is described anywhere in the paper; the E2E RAG is a training-free integration of pretrained models.

3) Retrieved text fed with spoken query to the S2S model — CONFIRMED. "the system feeds both the spoken query and the retrieved content into the end-to-end speech-to-speech dialogue model." ("Concatenated" is a faithful rendering of "feeds both … into.")

4) Gains — CONFIRMED, matching the paper's own stated figures: "our system has a significant improvement over the native dialogue model without RAG (~20% improvement on HotpotQA)" and "~43% improvement on RGB-zh." (Table I absolute answer-accuracy values: HotpotQA 0.27→0.43; RGB-zh 0.17→0.54.)

5) Latency — CONFIRMED verbatim: "our end-to-end retrieval system can reduce the retrieval time of the cascade system (ASR RAG) to 1/4 on both the English and Chinese datasets (reducing 0.4s to 0.08s)."

Minor imprecisions that do NOT refute the claim: (a) SONAR is a joint speech-AND-text encoder, so calling it a "speech encoder" is slightly narrow, but the claim separately states both modalities enter one shared space, capturing the point; (b) the paper's stated ~20%/~43% are absolute-point improvements and don't exactly equal the Table I deltas (16 and 37 points), but the claim reproduces the paper's own reported percentages faithfully.

Source located and read: arXiv 2506.05690v3 (HTML full text + abstract). The arXiv ID and version cited are correct and pin the intended paper; a web search for the cited title returns only this same paper, so there is no title ambiguity about which source is meant. Every substantive element of the claim is directly supported by verbatim/near-verbatim text:

(1) Neither paradigm wins outright — paper's premise is "GraphRAG frequently underperforms vanilla RAG on many real-world tasks," and it maps each to distinct task regimes.
(2) Graph wins reasoning/sense-making/narrative — "GraphRAG models show a clear advantage in complex reasoning, Contextual Summarize, and creative generation" and its ability "to connect information across distant text segments, crucial for multi-hop reasoning and comprehensive summarization."
(3) Flat RAG matches/beats on fact retrieval with 83.2% — "Basic RAG is comparable to or outperforms GraphRAG in simple fact retrieval tasks" and "RAG excels at retrieving discrete facts for simple questions ... achieving 83.2% Evidence Recall" (Table 3, Section 4.2, Level 1 / Fact Retrieval, RAG w/ rerank on the novel dataset).
(4) Redundant/noisy info mechanism — "GraphRAG's extra graph-based processing may introduce redundant or noisy information for simpler queries, degrading answer quality." (near-verbatim to the claim's "injects redundant/noisy info on simple queries").
(5) Task-shape is the deciding variable — "The primary distinction between these two paradigms lies in their handling of contextual depth. RAG excels in scenarios requiring rapid access to discrete information, while GraphRAG emphasizes deep contextual analysis for tasks requiring nuanced understanding of interconnected data."

The claimant's paraphrases ("single-passage" for the paper's Level-1 discrete-fact questions; "synthesis-into-narrative" for "creative generation"; "task-shape" for the paper's "contextual depth"/task-complexity axis) are faithful, not distortions. Adversarial checks (searching for a distinct paper of the cited name, checking the 83.2% attribution) did not surface any contradiction.
correction: Substance fully verified; one citation-hygiene error to fix. The cited paper TITLE is wrong: arXiv 2506.05690v3 is actually titled "When to use Graphs in RAG: A Comprehensive Analysis for Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation" (Xiang, Wu, Zhang, Chen, Hong, Huang, Su), not "When Do We Need Graph Structures in RAG?". The arXiv ID and version (2506.05690v3, 2025) are correct. Minor precision note: the 83.2% is Evidence Recall for RAG (with rerank) on Level-1 fact-retrieval questions per Table 3 — "single-passage" is the claimant's reasonable gloss, not the paper's exact term.

evidence: Located and read the cited source (arXiv:2605.27123, "Rethinking Agentic RAG: Toward LLM-Driven Logical Retrieval Beyond Embeddings," Zeng et al., Fudan/Shanghai Kingstar) at https://arxiv.org/html/2605.27123v1. Every load-bearing element of the claim matches: (1) Method (named LogicalRAG) has the LLM emit "Lucene-style query-string syntax over the title and content fields," combining terms with AND/OR/NOT, quoted phrases for exact matching, and field targeting (title:"..."); the inverted index selects candidates and "BM25 is then used to rank documents within this candidate set." (2) Training-free confirmed: LogicalRAG "does not introduce a new scoring function or retrieval architecture," running a frozen off-the-shelf LLM at inference time with no training/fine-tuning. (3) KILT-scale corpus parity confirmed exactly: "the average LLM-as-a-Judge accuracy is 0.717 for LogicalRAG and 0.716 for Agentic Hybrid"; the "Agentic Hybrid" baseline is "hybrid sparse-dense retrieval merged by reciprocal rank fusion" (= dense-sparse). (4) 41x build: 1.27 h vs 52.02 h ("about 41x higher offline construction time"). (5) 2.3x throughput: 152.5 vs 66.6 QPS at concurrency 16 ("2.3x higher throughput"). (6) 3.1x latency: 74.9 ms vs 230.5 ms ("3.1x lower mean latency"). (7) 35% hallucination reduction in the answer-unavailable (evidence-absent) evaluation: 0.128 -> 0.083 (~35.2% relative). (8) Gains grow with capability: "With Qwen3.5-4B, LogicalRAG trailed Agentic Hybrid by about three points... As the agent became stronger, LogicalRAG improved rapidly and the gap... largely closed. With Qwen3.5-Plus, the two methods reached near parity," attributed to "stronger agents can more effectively exploit the high-control action space." Two immaterial notes: the actual title includes the word "Toward" (claim drops it), and at the strongest model LogicalRAG only reaches parity (+0.001), so "gains growing" denotes a shrinking relative deficit rather than a positive lead — but the paper's own framing supports the claim's direction. None of these affect the substance.

All substantive numbers verified against both cited sources.

HippoRAG 2 (arXiv 2502.14802, "From RAG to Memory: Non-Parametric Continual Learning for LLMs"): MuSiQue = 11,656 passages (Table 1). Indexing token cost for MuSiQue (Table 12): HippoRAG 2 = 9.2M, LightRAG = 68.5M, GraphRAG = 115.5M input tokens — exact match, ordering intact. LightRAG average F1 = 6.6 across all datasets (Table 2) — exact match. Noise mechanism verbatim: "Although both GraphRAG and LightRAG use a KG just like our HippoRAG 2 approach, our KG is used to aid in the retrieval process rather than to expand the retrieval corpus itself. This allows HippoRAG 2 to introduce less LLM-generated noise, which deteriorates the performance of these methods in single and multi-hop QA tasks." — directly supports "LLM-generated graph noise can actively hurt when the KG expands the corpus."

Survey (arXiv 2506.05690): Global-GraphRAG "reaches a prompt size of up to 4x10^4 tokens"; LightRAG "produces lengthy prompts (~10^4 tokens)"; HippoRAG2 "maintains a more compact prompt size (~10^3 tokens)." Per-query ordering (GraphRAG > LightRAG > HippoRAG2) matches the build-cost ordering, so "restated by the survey" is accurate. The claim correctly keeps build cost (from HippoRAG2 paper) distinct from per-query overhead (from survey) without conflating the two metrics.

I tried to refute the token counts, the 6.6 F1, and the corpus-expansion/noise mechanism; each is present verbatim in the sources. Only a minor, non-substantive citation-label imperfection was found (see correction) — it does not affect any load-bearing figure or conclusion.
correction: Minor citation-label note (does not change the verdict): the survey at arXiv 2506.05690 is actually titled "When to use Graphs in RAG: A Comprehensive Analysis for Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation" (a.k.a. GraphRAG-Bench), not "When Do We Need Graph Structures in RAG." The arXiv ID is correct and unambiguously identifies the right paper; the claim's title is a loose paraphrase. All numerical and mechanistic content is fully confirmed.

evidence:
Opened arXiv:2510.02044 ("Stream RAG: Instant and Accurate Spoken Dialogue Systems with Streaming Tool Usage", Arora et al.) — both the abstract page and the full HTML. Every element of the claim is directly supported:

(1) Parallel-with-speech triggering: Abstract verbatim — "reduces user-perceived latency by predicting tool queries in parallel with user speech, even before the user finishes speaking."

(2) Three primitives: Trigger = "When to initiate a new tool query"; Threads = "The number of parallel tool query threads"; Reflector = "The module that determines whether intermediate tool results are sufficient for generating the final output." Matches the claim's definitions.

(3) Trigger has two settings = fixed-interval vs model-learned: verbatim — "we introduce two complementary approaches... a fixed-interval trigger method and a model-based trigger method"; "the trigger is set to fire tool calls at fixed chunk intervals" (3.2.1) vs "the trigger is learned: the model is trained to autonomously determine the optimal moments" (3.2.2). Fixed-interval "requires NO post-training; operates as plug-and-play at inference time"; model-triggered "requires post-training." NO_QUERY token predicted "when no new tool call is needed"; decision made "after processing each 500ms block." All match.

(4) AudioCRAG accuracy: baseline closed-book 11.1% vs model-triggered 34.2% absolute ("up to 200% relative, from 11.1% to 34.2% absolute"). Match.

(5) Latency reductions: "20.7% reductions in first-token latency on the synthetic benchmark"; 53.4% for AudioCRAG-Human. Match.

(6) Fixed-interval with no model update: "the Fixed-Interval Streaming RAG approach already reduces tool usage latency... by 10.7%" (no post-training). Match.

All load-bearing claims verified against RAPTOR (arXiv 2401.18059, ICLR 2024) via its abstract and HTML full text. (1) Recursive cluster+summarize bottom-up tree with multi-level retrieval — abstract: "recursively embedding, clustering, and summarizing chunks of text, constructing a tree with differing levels of summarization from the bottom up" and "retrieves from this tree, integrating information across lengthy documents at different levels of abstraction." (2) The +20% figure is verbatim: "by coupling RAPTOR retrieval with the use of GPT-4, we can improve the best performance on the QuALITY benchmark by 20% in absolute accuracy." (3) Similarity-only integration confirmed: both retrieval strategies rank nodes by cosine similarity — Tree Traversal ("Compute the cosine similarity between the query embedding and the embeddings of all nodes present at this initial layer") and Collapsed Tree ("Calculate the cosine similarity between the query embedding and the embeddings of all nodes present in the collapsed set C"); no graph/entity/relational integration mechanism is described. Clustering uses GMM + soft clustering + UMAP, consistent with a similarity-based method. (4) "Foundational hierarchical baseline" and "later criticized as its limitation" are the claimant's framing, not paper self-statements, but they do not contradict the source and correctly attribute the criticism to later work; they are consistent with how graph-RAG successors position against similarity-only retrieval. Could not parse the raw PDF (binary), but the arXiv abstract page and arxiv.org/html/2401.18059v1 provided the exact quotes needed.

Verified against the two cited primary sources (both opened).

CONFIRMED (Chroma "Context Rot" report, trychroma.com/research/context-rot): 18 models evaluated, including GPT-4.1 (+mini/nano), Claude Opus 4 / Sonnet 4, Gemini 2.5 Pro/Flash, and Qwen3-235B/32B/8B. Direct quotes: "LLMs are typically presumed to process context uniformly... this assumption does not hold"; "model performance grows increasingly unreliable as input length grows." So the "18 models / non-uniform context / degrades with input length" portion is accurate.

REFUTED — the mitigation clause is unsupported by, and actively contradicted by, the cited sources: The Chroma report DID test needle position and found NO lost-in-the-middle U-shape: "Testing across 11 needle positions, we find no notable variation in performance for this specific NIAH task." Its actual positional result is the opposite/counterintuitive one — "structural coherence consistently hurts model performance" (shuffled haystacks outperform coherent ones). Chroma makes no start/end edge-placement recommendation. arXiv 2510.10276 ("Lost in the Middle: An Emergent Property from Information Retrieval Demands in LLMs") studies small GPT-2/Llama models trained FROM SCRATCH — not 2025 frontier models — and explains the U-shape as an emergent training artifact; it gives no edge-placement mitigation advice.

The specific "position 5-15 death zone / place at first-or-last positions to keep accuracy high" wording surfaces only in secondary blog syntheses (Morph, particula.tech), which import the classic result and misattribute it to Chroma — the exact "search-snippet not opened" hazard. The edge-placement U-shape mitigation is the finding of the ORIGINAL 2023 paper (Liu et al., arXiv 2307.03172), not either cited 2025 source.
correction: Split the claim. Accurate part (keep, cite Chroma context-rot): across 18 frontier models (GPT-4.1, Claude 4, Gemini 2.5, Qwen3) context is not used uniformly and reliability degrades non-uniformly as input length grows. INCORRECT attribution (fix): neither cited 2025 source supports "placing top-scoring documents at start/end edges mitigates it." Chroma explicitly found no notable needle-position variation in its NIAH task (and found shuffled/incoherent haystacks improve performance — the opposite of a coherence-based fix); arXiv 2510.10276 studies small from-scratch models and only explains the U-shape mechanism. The edge-placement (primacy/recency U-shape) mitigation should be cited to the original 2023 "Lost in the Middle" paper (Liu et al., arXiv 2307.03172), not to Chroma context-rot or arXiv 2510.10276. Also avoid conflating length-based "context rot" (Chroma's finding) with positional "lost in the middle" (Liu 2023 / the 2510.10276 mechanism study) — they are distinct phenomena.

All numbers and architecture claims confirmed.

"ReasoningBank: Scaling Agent Self-Evolving with Reasoning Memory" (arXiv:2509.25140, 29 Sep 2025; Ouyang, Yan et al.) 'distills generalizable reasoning strategies from an agent's self-judged successful and failed experiences' into structured memory items retrieved at test time (not raw traces), for self-evolving agents; MaTTS yields up to 34.2% success-rate gain / 16.0% fewer steps. The CBR companion, "Review of Case-Based Reasoning for LLM Agents..." (arXiv:2504.06943, Apr 2025; Hatalis, Christou, Kondapalli), formalizes the canonical 4-R cycle ('retrieval of similar cases, reuse/adaptation..., revision..., and retention of new solutions') and represents cases as exemplar triples: 'Memory banks in LLM agents function as repositories of demonstration exemplars, typically in the form of (question, chain-of-thought, answer) triples.' Matches claim precisely.

Primary source: 'When to use Graphs in RAG: A Comprehensive Analysis for Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation' (arXiv 2506.05690; v1 6 Jun 2025, v2 rev 22 Feb 2026). All three numbers appear verbatim in the Introduction (para 2): (a) 'GraphRAG achieves 13.4% lower accuracy on the Natural Question compared to vanilla RAG'; (b) 'particularly poor performance on time-sensitive queries (e.g., 16.6% accuracy drop for questions requiring real-time knowledge updates)'; (c) 'While graph-based retrieval improves reasoning depth by only 4.5% on HotpotQA's multi-hop questions, it introduces 2.3x higher latency on average.' Core cost-tradeoff CONFIRMED from primary papers. HiRAG ('Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Hierarchical Knowledge', arXiv 2503.10150, v1 13 Mar 2025): offline indexing is more expensive but modest (~$7.55 on the Mix dataset with DeepSeek-V3) and 'HiRAG does not cost any tokens for retrieval' (~zero online retrieval token cost). ArchRAG ('Attributed Community-based Hierarchical Retrieval-Augmented Generation', arXiv 2502.09891, AAAI): emphasizes low online token cost, cutting HotpotQA online tokens ~250x vs GraphRAG-Global (1,394M -> 5.1M). BUT the two illustrative figures are secondary and not primary-verifiable: the '$10-15 to index 800KB with GPT-4.1 (>90% cheaper with mini/Flash)' is a Medium-blog estimate with no primary paper; and 'LightRAG 757M tokens on HotpotQA vs 62M naive' could not be located in any primary source and conflicts with a primary token-cost study (TERAG, arXiv 2509.18667, Table 3), which measures LightRAG on HotpotQA at ~44.6M total tokens (38.8M in + 5.9M out), not 757M (absolute token counts are setup/subset-dependent).
correction: The HiRAG offline-heavy/online-~zero and ArchRAG low-online-token claims are solid (primary). The two specific cost numbers are secondary-source illustrations: the $10-15/800KB GPT-4.1 figure is a blog estimate (no primary), and the '757M vs 62M naive' LightRAG figure is unconfirmed in any primary source and inconsistent with the closest primary token-cost measurement (TERAG reports LightRAG ~44.6M on HotpotQA). Treat both numbers as unverified, setup-dependent estimates rather than established primary facts.

support: WavRAG CONFIRMED ('WavRAG: Audio-Integrated Retrieval Augmented Generation for Spoken Dialogue Models', arXiv 2502.14727, v1 20 Feb 2025): 'we propose the WavRetriever to facilitate the retrieval from a text-audio hybrid knowledge base' and reports 'comparable retrieval performance while delivering a 10x acceleration' vs ASR-Text RAG. PlanRAG-Audio CONFIRMED to exist and use plan-then-retrieve ('PlanRAG-Audio: Planning and Retrieval Augmented Generation for Long-form Audio Understanding', arXiv 2605.20414, CMU + Amazon AGI, submitted 19 May 2026): Stage-2 explicit retrieval planning specifies which modality representations, filters, and stream joins are required before retrieval. HOWEVER the claim that both 'remain flat hybrid indexes' is inaccurate for PlanRAG-Audio, which uses 'a structured, time-aligned audio database D(a) consisting of modality-specific metadata streams' (transcript/speaker/emotion/sound-event streams, temporally aligned by diarization), queried via SQL/Common-Table-Expression joins.
correction: The load-bearing point holds: neither WavRAG nor PlanRAG-Audio imposes a graph or hierarchical-community organization (like GraphRAG/HiRAG/ArchRAG). But 'they remain flat hybrid indexes' mischaracterizes PlanRAG-Audio, which is a structured, time-aligned, modality-partitioned relational store (SQL/CTE queries over transcript/speaker/emotion/sound-event streams), not a flat index. WavRAG is the flat hybrid text-audio index; PlanRAG-Audio adds explicit relational structure short of a graph/hierarchy.

support: Primary source: 'Long Context vs. RAG for LLMs: An Evaluation and Revisits' (arXiv 2501.01880, v1, submitted 27 Dec 2024; Xinze Li, Yixin Cao, Yubo Ma, Aixin Sun). Abstract supports all four sub-claims verbatim: 'LC generally outperforms RAG in question-answering benchmarks, especially for Wikipedia-based questions'; 'RAG has advantages in dialogue-based and general question queries'; 'Summarization-based retrieval performs comparably to LC, while chunk-based retrieval lags behind'; and '...the overlooked importance of context relevance in existing studies.'

Primary source: 'REARANK: Reasoning Re-ranking Agent via Reinforcement Learning' (arXiv 2505.20046, v1, 26 May 2025). GRPO confirmed (Sec 3.2: 'we employ the simple Grouped Policy Optimization (GRPO) algorithm'). Data confirmed (Sec 4.1: '179 queries from MSMARCO-V2', sampled 20 candidates x 50 repeats -> '12k training instances'). Gains vs RankQwen2.5-7B baseline: Table 1 BEIR avg 50.10 -> 54.59 (+4.49), TREC-DL19 68.25 -> 74.16 (+5.91); Table 2 BRIGHT avg 15.0 -> 17.7 (+2.7), and Rearank-7B (17.7) surpasses RankGPT-4 (16.8). Built on Qwen2.5-7B. Every numeric claim matches.

CORE part CONFIRMED: 'Less Is More: Elevating RAG via Performance-Driven Context Compression' (arXiv 2508.19282, v1 24 Aug 2025, latest v4). It 'directly utilizes task performance as a feedback signal to iteratively refine the compressor policy' (RL driven by downstream answer performance); on Natural Questions it beats no-compression full-context and LongLLMLingua (CORE 41.02 EM vs full-context 38.03 vs LongLLMLingua 33.65), and at ~3% compression improves avg EM by +3.3 vs full documents. LongLLMLingua part CONFIRMED against v1: arXiv 2310.06839 v1 (10 Oct 2023) abstract states 'on NaturalQuestions... a performance boost of up to 17.1%... with ~4x fewer tokens' (note the later v2 revised this to 21.4%). LLMLingua-2 part is where the claim errs: arXiv 2403.12968 confirms it is a Transformer/BERT-family (XLM-RoBERTa/mBERT) token-classification compressor, '3x-6x faster than existing prompt compression methods', with OOD/robust generalization — but it is NOT training-free.
correction: LLMLingua-2 is not 'training-free': it is a token classifier TRAINED via data distillation from an LLM (arXiv 2403.12968: 'propose a data distillation procedure to derive knowledge from an LLM to compress prompts'). The original LLMLingua (2310.05736) is the training-free, perplexity-based method; LLMLingua-2 requires training. The '3-6x faster', 'OOD robustness', and 'frozen-at-inference token classifier' descriptors are correct, and LongLLMLingua's +17.1% at ~4x (v1) is correct.

support: Primary source: 'Beyond RAG vs. Long-Context: Learning Distraction-Aware Retrieval for Efficient Knowledge Grounding' (arXiv 2509.21865, v1 26 Sep 2025, v2 rev 25 Feb 2026). Policy-gradient RL confirmed: the retriever pi_theta is trained via the likelihood-ratio/log-derivative estimator 'theta_{k+1} = theta_k + gamma * r_psi(q,R,y) * grad log pi_theta', learning to select passage sets that mitigate distractor interference. Beats both baselines with fewer tokens (Table 1, 32K setting): LDAR 70.00 (0.467 token ratio) vs long-context 58.62 (1.000) vs RAG 62.12 (0.094); 128K: LDAR 61.55 (0.250) vs long-context 43.65 (1.000) — 'significantly better performance... while using only about half the token usage of the long-context approach.' Minor nuance: RAG uses fewer tokens than LDAR (0.094 vs 0.467) but scores lower; 'fewer tokens' in the claim is relative to long-context, which holds.

Primary source: 'Online-Optimized RAG for Tool Use and Function Calling' (arXiv 2509.20415, v1 24 Sep 2025, v2 26 Sep 2025; Yu Pan, Xiaocheng Li, Hanzhao Wang). Mechanism CONFIRMED: importance-weighted SGD (gradient g_{t,i} carries a 1/p_{t,i_t} inverse-propensity correction); 'if the choice is correct... the update moves theta toward q_t, increasing similarity. If incorrect, the update moves away from q_t.' Benchmarks UltraTool, ToolRet (Web/Code/Customized), FiQA, MultiHopRAG all present; 'negligible per-query latency' / plug-and-play CONFIRMED. However the '+3-9% Recall@10/NDCG@10' range does not hold uniformly: UltraTool (+3.26 to +8.05 R@10), ToolRet-Code (+5.37 to +9.56), ToolRet-Customized (+5.59 to +6.73) fall in range, but ToolRet-Web (+1.29 to +1.63 R@10 / +0.94 to +2.18 N@10) and FiQA (~+1.6 R@10 / ~+2.2 N@10) are below 3%, and MultiHopRAG is reported as end-to-end QA accuracy (0.55 -> 0.68), not Recall@10/NDCG@10.
correction: Mechanism, benchmarks, and negligible-latency claims are correct, but the gains are not a uniform +3-9%: retrieval gains span roughly +1% to +9.5%, with FiQA and ToolRet-Web at only ~+1-2%, and MultiHopRAG's improvement is an end-to-end QA-accuracy gain (0.55->0.68), not a Recall@10/NDCG@10 delta. State the range as ~+1% to +9.5% (largest on UltraTool/ToolRet-Code) rather than +3-9% across all four.

support: Primary source: 'Never Come Up Empty: Adaptive HyDE Retrieval for Improving LLM Developer Support' (arXiv 2507.16754, v1, 22 Jul 2025; Fangjian Lei, Mariam El Mezouar, Shayan Noei, Ying Zou). Abstract/body confirm: 'design and evaluate 7 different RAG pipelines and 63 pipeline variants'; the HyDE + full-answer-context pipeline (HB1) 'performs best in retrieving and answering similar content'; for novel questions it works by 'automatically lowering the similarity threshold during retrieval, thereby increasing the chance of finding partially relevant context'; and it 'consistently outperforms zero-shot baselines across models' by LLM-as-a-judge on helpfulness/correctness/detail. The 4 open-source LLMs are named: Granite-3.1-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3, Qwen3-8B, and LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct. No hard numbers in abstract, as the claim notes. All sub-claims confirmed.

The two quantitative claims check out against the cited 2025-26 syntheses (Michael Brenndoerfer, mbrenndoerfer.com/writing/hybrid-search-bm25-dense-retrieval-fusion, and digitalapplied.com/blog/hybrid-search-bm25-vector-reranking-reference-2026), which report the same WANDS numbers from Doug Turnbull's Mar-2025 study. (1) 'Convex Combination (CC) with alpha=0.5 (equal weighting of BM25 and dense scores) achieving Recall@5 of 0.726, outperforming RRF (k=60) at 0.695' — matches exactly (they add that RRF k=10 is the best RRF variant at 0.716). (2) '7.4% NDCG lift over either alone' on WANDS — confirmed (tuned hybrid ~0.7497 vs BM25 0.6983 / dense KNN 0.6953). (3) 'RRF needs no score calibration' — confirmed: 'RRF sidesteps this entirely by operating only on rank positions — no normalization required.'
correction: The sub-claim 'convex blending uses raw scores' is the opposite of what the primary sources say. They state convex/linear combination requires min-max NORMALIZED scores; mixing RAW scores is explicitly the failure mode ('Mixing raw scores gives BM25 dominant weight by default' because BM25 is unbounded while cosine is in [-1,1]). Correct statement: RRF is rank-based and needs no calibration, whereas convex/linear blending operates on SCORE values that must be normalized (e.g., min-max) before combining, not raw scores.

support: All three components verified from the primary papers. (a) ColBERT/late-interaction MaxSim: the ColPali paper (arXiv:2407.01449, 'ColPali: Efficient Document Retrieval with Vision Language Models', v3) restates the operator: 'LI(q,d)=sum over i in [1,Nq] of max over j in [1,Nd] of <Eq(i)|Ed(j)>' — i.e., sum over query vectors of the max dot-product with each document token vector. (b) PLAID: arXiv:2205.09707 'PLAID: An Efficient Engine for Late Interaction Retrieval' (May 2022, SIGIR/CIKM) states latency reductions of 'up to 7x on a GPU and 45x on a CPU' relative to vanilla ColBERTv2, via a novel centroid-interaction mechanism (bag of centroids) plus centroid pruning. (c) ColPali: default variant uses PaliGemma's vision encoder producing 1024 image patch embeddings per page, D=128 vectors, and does retrieval by 'directly embedding the images of the document pages,' bypassing OCR.

All five example systems verified. IRCoT interleaves retrieval with chain-of-thought reasoning (retrieve after each CoT sentence). FLARE (arXiv:2305.06983, 'Active Retrieval Augmented Generation', EMNLP 2023) triggers retrieval when the predicted upcoming sentence contains low-probability/low-confidence tokens. Self-RAG (arXiv:2310.11511) uses trained reflection tokens. Adaptive-RAG (arXiv:2403.14403) routes with a smaller-LM (T5-Large) complexity classifier. Stop-RAG (arXiv:2510.14337 'Stop-RAG: Value-Based Retrieval Control for Iterative RAG', Oct 2025, NeurIPS 2025 MTI-LLM Workshop) casts iterative RAG as a finite-horizon MDP and uses a value-based controller trained with Q(lambda) targets to decide when to stop — i.e., a value function. The prompting/confidence/training-based paradigm grouping is an accurate framing.

LangChain's self-query retriever docs: 'A self-querying retriever ... uses an LLM to write a structured query from any natural language query and then applies that structured query to its underlying vector store,' using the query for semantic similarity while 'extracting filters from the user query on document metadata and executing those filters' — matches the claim's 'semantic vector plus structured metadata filters, then executes a filtered vector search.' Minor nuance: LangChain emits a semantic query STRING (subsequently embedded to a vector) plus a metadata filter, not a pre-computed vector, but this is immaterial to the claim's mechanism.

The qualitative mechanism is well-supported by primary/academic sources: agentic RAG exposes retrieval as a tool the agent calls (function-schema tool description, e.g. 'retrieves up to 5 chunks relevant to the query') and treats retrieval strategy as a learned policy — Search-R1, ReSearch, ToolRL/ToRL, and the SoK on Agentic RAG (arXiv:2603.07379) train agents via RL to choose retrieval behavior and show gains over fixed/static retrieval. So 'retrieval as a tool-call via structured function schemas' and 'learned policy over retriever/top-k/reranker depth/chunk size' are CONFIRMED.
correction: The specific figure '15-20% retrieval-quality lift over static configurations' could not be traced to any primary source; it appears only in vendor/blog syntheses (labelyourdata, futureagi) as flagged in the source hint. No locatable paper reports a 15-20% retrieval-quality improvement for early agentic-RAG systems as a general result. Treat the mechanism as confirmed but the magnitude as unsubstantiated (blog-sourced, unverifiable).

support: All three verified. Mem0 (arXiv:2504.19413, 'Mem0: Building Production-Ready AI Agents with Scalable Long-Term Memory', Chhikara et al. 2025): update phase uses a tool-call mechanism deciding ADD / UPDATE / DELETE / NOOP over salient facts extracted in the extraction phase (exact four operations, with the definitions given). A-Mem (arXiv:2502.12110, 'A-MEM: Agentic Memory for LLM Agents', Xu et al., Feb 2025): Zettelkasten-inspired, with a 'Memory Evolution' component where new memories trigger updates to the contextual representations/attributes of existing linked historical notes — i.e., note-evolution rewriting linked neighbors. Agentic Memory (arXiv:2601.01885, 'Agentic Memory: Learning Unified Long-Term and Short-Term Memory Management for LLM Agents', Yi Yu et al., Jan 2026, ACL 2026): exposes store/retrieve/update/summarize/discard as callable tool actions, trained via a three-stage pipeline (SFT warm-up -> task-level outcome-reward RL -> step-level/step-wise GRPO for dense per-action credit assignment). The survey 'Memory for Autonomous LLM Agents' (arXiv:2603.07670) frames all three consistently.

Self-RAG (arXiv:2310.11511, 'Self-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection', Asai et al. 2023): Table 1 defines exactly four reflection-token types — Retrieve (whether to retrieve), IsRel/ISREL (relevance), IsSup/ISSUP (support/grounding), IsUse/ISUSE (utility, 5-point). These are 'inserted offline into the original corpus by a trained critic model' C (trained on GPT-4-distilled supervision), which annotates training data before the generator M is trained; the critic is not needed at inference. Open-RAG (arXiv:2410.01782, 'Open-RAG: Enhanced Retrieval-Augmented Reasoning with Open-Source LLMs', EMNLP 2024 Findings): 'transforms an arbitrary dense LLM into a parameter-efficient sparse mixture of experts (MoE) model capable of handling complex reasoning tasks' incl. multi-hop. Both systems are trained, so the scoped conclusion 'this reflect/verify primitive requires weight training' holds for Self-RAG/Open-RAG as stated (adaptive reflection can also be done via prompting more broadly, but the two cited systems do require training).
correction: Minor scoping caveat only: the generalized clause 'The adaptive reflect/verify primitive therefore REQUIRES weight training' is true for the Self-RAG/Open-RAG family cited, but adaptive reflection in general is not universally training-dependent (e.g., prompting-based reflection). The factual core about both cited papers is correct.

support: CRAG (arXiv:2401.15884, 'Corrective Retrieval Augmented Generation', Yan et al., v3 Oct 2024). Confirmed: (a) a lightweight retrieval evaluator grades retrieved docs and returns a confidence degree mapped to three actions — Correct, Incorrect, Ambiguous. (b) A decompose-then-recompose algorithm splits documents into 'knowledge strips' ('If a retrieved result is as short as one or two sentences, it is regarded as an individual strip, otherwise ... split into smaller units'). (c) Large-scale web search is integrated as an extension when the Incorrect action fires. (d) Ablation on PopQA triggering one action for all instances (Table 11): only-Correct 52.4, only-Incorrect 47.0, only-Ambiguous 52.7 (LLaMA2-hf-7b), showing no single fixed action matches the adaptive routing and that the decomposed-refinement / web-search / evaluator components each contribute. The claim's four-way framing (routing + decomposed filtering + web expansion + correctness verification) is a fair paraphrase, noting 'correctness verification' and 'routing' both refer to the same retrieval evaluator.

Adaptive-RAG (arXiv:2403.14403, 'Adaptive-RAG: Learning to Adapt Retrieval-Augmented LLMs through Question Complexity', Jeong et al., NAACL 2024): trains a smaller LM classifier — implemented as T5-Large — to predict query complexity and route among three strategies: no-retrieval (simple), single-step retrieval (moderate), and multi-step/iterative retrieval (complex), with labels auto-collected from model outcomes and dataset biases; it 'seamlessly adapts' to match the expensive always-multi-step approach on complex queries while saving cost on easy ones. SKR ('Self-Knowledge guided Retrieval augmentation', Wang et al., EMNLP Findings 2023) routes based on the model's apparent self-knowledge (retrieve only when the model likely does not already know the answer) — accurately characterized. Cross-referenced via 'A Systematic Review of RAG Systems' (arXiv:2507.18910).

All five cited papers verified as real with correct arXiv IDs and substantially correct mechanism descriptions. (1) DeepSieve 'Information Sieving via LLM-as-a-Knowledge-Router' arXiv:2507.22050 (v4 1 Mar 2026; EACL Findings 2026) — modular pipeline with components decomposition, routing, retrieval, REFLEXION, and fusion; routes sub-questions to knowledge sources. ✓ (2) arXiv:2505.22095 'Learning to Route Queries Across Knowledge Bases for Step-wise Retrieval-Augmented Reasoning' (R1-Router, OpenBMB) — RL via Step-GRPO with step-wise rewards; routes among multiple KBs (Text/Text-Image/Table retrievers) for MLLMs. ✓ (3) RAGRouter arXiv:2505.23052 'Learning to Route Queries to Multiple Retrieval-Augmented Language Models' — document embeddings + learnable per-LLM 'RAG capability embedding' with contrastive learning. ✓ (4) GraphRouter arXiv:2410.03834 (ICLR 2025) 'A Graph-based Router for LLM Selections' — LLM selection framed as edge/link prediction over a heterogeneous graph. (5) RealRoute arXiv:2604.20860 'Dynamic Query Routing System via Retrieve-then-Verify Paradigm' — retrieve-then-verify. ✓
correction: Two nuances the survey sentence blurs: (a) GraphRouter's heterogeneous graph nodes are TASK, QUERY, and LLM — there is no 'source' node, so 'query-model-source graph' should read task-query-LLM (model). (b) RAGRouter and GraphRouter are LLM/MODEL routers (which model answers), not knowledge-source selectors, and RealRoute deliberately AVOIDS source prediction (parallel source-agnostic retrieval). So the umbrella 'source selection before retrieval' cleanly fits only DeepSieve and R1-Router; it is a loose framing for the other three.

support: 'Deep Research: A Survey of Autonomous Research Agents' arXiv:2508.12752 (18 Aug 2025, Zhang et al.) defines FOUR core pipeline stages: Planning, Question Developing, Web Exploration, Report Generation — there is NO distinct 'verify' stage. Full-text (html v1) check: the survey does NOT describe a deterministic post-processing step that verifies every citation against retrieved sources, and makes NO mention of a separate 'citations agent' that inserts/repairs supports; Section 5.2 discusses generation-time 'faithful modeling' + 'conflict reasoning' and lists explicit source attribution only as a FUTURE DIRECTION. The Step-DeepResearch part IS supported: Step-DeepResearch Technical Report arXiv:2512.20491 (StepFun) proposes a 'Data Synthesis Strategy Based on Atomic Capabilities' reinforcing planning, information gathering, reflection, and report writing.
correction: The 'plan->search->synthesize->VERIFY' framing with a deterministic per-citation verification pass against retrieved sources and a separate citations agent that inserts/repairs supports is NOT attributable to the cited survey (whose stages are planning / question-developing / web-exploration / report-generation, with citation/attribution only a future direction, no verify stage and no citations agent). The Step-DeepResearch atomic-capabilities clause is confirmed (note its atomic set is four items — planning, information gathering, reflection, AND report writing).

support: RAGCap-Bench arXiv:2510.13910 'Benchmarking Capabilities of LLMs in Agentic Retrieval Augmented Generation Systems' (Lin, Zhang, Liu, Li). Confirmed: four capability categories = Planning, Evidence Extraction, Grounded Reasoning, Noise Robustness (Noise Robustness split into Noise-Abstain and Noise-Reliability). correction: The specific quantitative claim '~50x faster than full WebThinker workflows' is NOT in the paper (checked abstract, full html, and independent review). The paper only asserts efficiency QUALITATIVELY ('an efficient alternative to costly, time-consuming end-to-end QA evaluation') with no ~50x (or any) speed/cost multiplier. Drop or qualify the 50x figure; everything else in the claim is supported.

support: 'Online-Optimized RAG for Tool Use and Function Calling' arXiv:2509.20415 (submitted 24 Sep 2025, rev 26 Sep 2025; Pan, Li, Wang). A DEPLOYMENT-TIME framework that 'continually adapts retrieval embeddings from live interactions using minimal feedback (e.g., task success)' via 'lightweight online gradient updates with negligible per-query latency' and 'requires no changes to the underlying LLM'; explicitly 'plug-and-play' supporting single- and multi-hop tool use, 'dynamic tool inventories, and K-retrieval with re-ranking.' Every element of the claim (deployment-time online embedding updates, minimal live feedback, negligible latency, no LLM change, dynamic tool inventories, K-retrieval + rerank) matches verbatim.

(1) TARG arXiv:2511.09803 'Retrieval as a Decision: Training-Free Adaptive Gating for Efficient RAG' (Wang, Wei, Ling; Nov 2025) — a single-shot gate that decides when to retrieve using only a short no-context draft; from the draft's PREFIX LOGITS it computes uncertainty scores (mean token entropy / top1-top2 margin via monotone link / small-N variance) and triggers retrieval when above threshold; model-agnostic, 'requires no additional training or auxiliary heads.' ✓ (2) FLARE (Jiang et al., EMNLP 2023) 'Active Retrieval Augmented Generation' = Forward-Looking Active REtrieval, triggers retrieval on low-confidence anticipated tokens. ✓ (3) Unified Active Retrieval arXiv:2406.12534 — unifies four orthogonal criteria (intent/knowledge/time/self awareness) as plug-and-play classifiers governing retrieval timing. ✓ (4) SeaKR arXiv:2406.19215 — extracts self-aware uncertainty from LLM internal states, activates retrieval on high uncertainty. ✓ (5) SUGAR arXiv:2501.04899 — semantic/context-entropy-guided adaptive retrieval (whether + single vs multi-step). ✓ All 'when-to-retrieve before full decoding' / uncertainty-probe characterizations hold.

The cited primary source for the headline claim, arXiv:2510.25623, is 'Evaluating the Role of Verifiers in Test-Time Scaling for LEGAL Reasoning Tasks' (EMNLP NLLP Workshop; legal MCQA, 5 benchmarks, 7 reward models). The secondary clause IS correct: Reason and Verify arXiv:2603.10143 ('A Framework for Faithful RAG') adds a rationale-generation module + eight-category faithfulness-verification taxonomy; FVA-RAG arXiv:2512.07015 ('Falsification-Verification Alignment for Mitigating Sycophantic Hallucinations') is a falsification-first architecture retrieving counter-evidence.
correction: The headline is backwards for its cited source: 2510.25623 finds self-consistency/majority-vote is a STRONG baseline and verifier-guided selection gives no benefit (or a decrease) for larger models — not 'higher accuracy at lower k than self-consistency.' It uses trained reward models (not 'prompting-based verifiers need no training') and reports no '1-3x fewer tokens' number. Only the 'Reason-and-Verify and FVA-RAG add faithfulness/falsification-verification passes over RAG outputs' clause is accurate.
